title: On Ownership
description: Own the outcome, not the method.
content:
What does it mean to own something? Most leaders answer that question incorrectly. We hear ownership and think control. "I own it, so I decide." I choose the method. I set the path. But that's not how teams work.

To own something is to be responsible for the outcome, not control every turn. The outcome is yours, but the method belongs to the team. The owner listens, integrates, adapts and removes obstacles to keep the outcome on track.

That's why ownership is better understood as stewardship.

Stewardship is the responsibility to care for something entrusted to you - not as personal property, but on behalf of the wider system it belongs to.

You can own a beehive, but you cannot own a bee. You care for the hive, protect it, and are responsible for its health. You can't tell a bee which flower to pollinate or restrict it to just the fields that you own. Your responsibility is to create the conditions for the hive to thrive.

Similarly, you can own a customer relationship, but you cannot own a customer. They have agency, choices, and the ability to leave. Your responsibility is to create the conditions for a long, happy customer relationship.

The same is true inside a team or an organisation. You can own an outcome, but you cannot own every decision, every person, or every step along the way.

That is the work of stewardship: staying responsible for the outcome while working through people, constraints, tradeoffs and changing conditions that you cannot control.

The point is not to give up the idea of ownership or sidestep responsibility. It is to understand ownership differently.

Nothing works as well as everything working together. Stewardship brings a broader obligation - not possession or control, but to create the conditions for success, and to make the whole ecosystem better for our involvement.

title: Two-state dark mode toggles
description: A persistent theme toggle should switch away from “yuck,” not make people choose a system setting.
content:
I keep returning to [Lea Verou’s argument](https://lea.verou.me/blog/2026/dark-mode-toggles/) that a persistent theme control needs only two visible states.

I’m not against tri-state controls on principle, but I agree with Lea: only developers think about `System`. Most people will never encounter a problem, and [Don’t Make Me Think](https://sensible.com/dont-make-me-think/) principles say to abstract confusing states away for the vast majority.

The two-state toggle implementation still has three values: system, light, and dark. But the toggle never actively selects “light” or “dark.” It simply switches away from “yuck”: whatever theme you’re looking at now.

I made a minimal reference implementation: [live demo](https://clyons.github.io/dark-mode-toggle-til/) and [source](https://github.com/clyons/dark-mode-toggle-til).

title: Animating a logo in Blender with a coding agent
description: Blender's Python API makes agent-generated 3D scenes surprisingly editable.
content:
Via [Simon Willison](https://til.simonwillison.net/llms/blender-coding-agents-macos) and others, I learned that LLMs are now very good at Blender. That makes sense: geometry, materials, and motion are ultimately math and code, and Blender has an extensive [Python API](https://docs.blender.org/api/current/index.html).

I needed an experiment, so I asked GPT-5.6 Sol:

> Use the already installed `/Applications/Blender` to render an extruded version of the Positive Intelligence symbol and logomark from positiveintelligence.com.

Finding and modelling the logo was easy. Sol found the artwork, imported it, removed the white background and registered trademark, extruded the remaining paths, and applied a reflective black material.

![The first extruded version of the Positive Intelligence logo](positive-intelligence-extruded-lockup.png)

Sol also created a normal `.blend` project containing the geometry, materials, camera, lights, and animation timeline. It can be opened and edited directly in Blender, just like a scene built by hand.

![The generated scene open for editing in Blender](blender-scene-editable.png)

## Futzing with light and motion

Lighting and motion were the tricky parts. I asked for a camera arc, a light moving in the opposite direction, and a more dynamic pan across the logo. Several iterations followed to remove a square reflection, make the light cross the whole face, and soften the final highlight.

The biggest visual improvement came from the backdrop. The curved wall used in a photography or film studio is called a [*cyclorama*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclorama_(theater)). Replacing separate floor and wall planes with one continuous cyclorama removed the horizon line and made the result feel much more like a studio shot.

The final animation uses a restrained camera arc, a circular moving light, a diffuse metallic reflection, and a cyclorama that cycles through four PQ brand colours.

<video src="positive-intelligence-logo-cinematic-v4.mp4?v=20260905" autoplay muted loop playsinline controls poster="cinematic-v4-keyframes.png" aria-label="Eight-second Positive Intelligence logo animation rendered in Blender"></video>

![Keyframes from the final PQ logo animation](cinematic-v4-keyframes.png)

The project lives at [clyons/gpt-5-6-sol-blender-positive-intelligence-logo](https://github.com/clyons/gpt-5-6-sol-blender-positive-intelligence-logo).

Scripts: [initial render](https://github.com/clyons/gpt-5-6-sol-blender-positive-intelligence-logo/blob/main/work/render_positive_intelligence.py), [first animation](https://github.com/clyons/gpt-5-6-sol-blender-positive-intelligence-logo/blob/main/work/render_positive_intelligence_animation.py), [v2](https://github.com/clyons/gpt-5-6-sol-blender-positive-intelligence-logo/blob/main/work/render_positive_intelligence_cinematic_v2.py), [v3](https://github.com/clyons/gpt-5-6-sol-blender-positive-intelligence-logo/blob/main/work/render_positive_intelligence_cinematic_v3.py), and [v4](https://github.com/clyons/gpt-5-6-sol-blender-positive-intelligence-logo/blob/main/work/render_positive_intelligence_cinematic_v4.py).

Files: [MP4](https://github.com/clyons/gpt-5-6-sol-blender-positive-intelligence-logo/blob/main/outputs/positive-intelligence-logo-cinematic-v4.mp4) and [Blender project](https://github.com/clyons/gpt-5-6-sol-blender-positive-intelligence-logo/blob/main/outputs/positive-intelligence-logo-cinematic-v4.blend).

title: Removing the Honda Clarity glove box damper
description: The clip releases backwards toward the engine, not by pulling it toward you.
content:
The damper clip releases by pushing the clip backwards toward the engine.

Pulling it toward you feels plausible, but it is the wrong direction and risks breaking the part.
